hypothesis: EVM bytecode's stack-based execution model is structurally isomorphic to Java bytecode, and adopting the SSA-based intermediate representation used in Java decompilation (which unifies def-use chains, type lattice propagation, and control-flow recovery into a single analysis pass) would eliminate the pipeline error-propagation problem that causes SigRec's function identification errors to cascade into type inference failures, and that Neural-FEBI's function boundary errors to cascade into CFG construction errors — i.e., a single SSA-construction pass can simultaneously recover function entries, parameter counts, and primitive types at precision ≥ the best specialized pipeline for each subtask.
rationale: In both Java bytecode and EVM bytecode, the fundamental challenge is recovering high-level structure (method/function boundaries, type signatures) from a stack-based, label-free instruction stream. The Java community settled on SSA as the universal intermediate representation precisely because it makes def-use chains explicit, enabling type inference (Gagnon et al., "Efficient Inference of Static Types for Java Bytecode") and control-flow recovery to operate on the same data structure rather than as sequential, error-propagating pipeline stages. The EVM literature currently treats function identification (Neural-FEBI, SigRec) and type inference (SigRec's TASE, Elipmoc's path-sensitive argument inference) as independent subproblems, which is architecturally exactly the mistake the Java decompilation community identified and solved two decades ago. If the isomorphism holds, an SSA-based EVM analysis would achieve simultaneous SoTA on all ABI subtasks.
supports_if: An SSA-based EVM analysis achieves F1 ≥ 0.95 on function entry identification (matching Neural-FEBI), F1 ≥ 0.90 on function boundary recovery (matching Neural-FEBI), and parameter-type precision ≥ 0.85 (matching SigRec's TASE), all from a single SSA-construction pass with no task-specific heuristics.
refutes_if: EVM-specific constructs (dynamic jumps via JUMPI with stack-computed targets, the absence of a static type system in EVM bytecode unlike JVM bytecode's descriptor-based method signatures, and the gas model that incentivizes code patterns with no Java analogue) make SSA construction either unsound for ≥ 10% of real-world contracts or produce an SSA representation that is too impoverished to recover parameter types at competitive precision.
motivating_papers: Efficient Inference of Static Types for Java Bytecode

hypothesis: The 4-byte function selector has a formal analogue in program analysis: it is a lossy hash of the ABI signature with a collision domain of 2^32, and the Java bytecode community's finding from obfuscation research (Dexpler) that call-site type constraints alone can recover method signatures even without method-name resolution implies that EVM parameter type recovery accuracy should be independent of 4byte.directory lookup success — call-site argument layouts and storage access patterns provide sufficient type constraints to recover arity, word-width, and dynamic-vs-static type distinctions without resolving the selector.
rationale: The lit-map identifies selector ambiguity as a fundamental limitation, but this framing conflates two distinct problems: (a) resolving which human-readable function name a selector corresponds to (which is indeed preimage-resistant), and (b) recovering how many parameters a function takes and what their EVM-level types are (which depends only on how the function body consumes calldata). Dexpler (Bartel et al.) demonstrated that in obfuscated Android bytecode, the loss of method names does not prevent recovery of parameter types because call sites and method bodies mutually constrain each other. The same structural relationship exists in EVM: internal JUMP targets, cross-contract CALL/CALLDATALOAD patterns, and storage access widths all reveal parameter layout constraints. If this independence holds, ABI recovery tools can decouple the selector-resolution problem (relying on external databases) from the type-recovery problem (relying on bytecode-internal analysis only).
supports_if: Ablating 4byte.directory lookup from SigRec or an equivalent tool reduces parameter-count accuracy by ≤ 5 percentage points and parameter-type accuracy by ≤ 10 percentage points, demonstrating that most type information is recoverable from bytecode-internal constraints alone.
refutes_if: Removing 4byte.directory lookup causes parameter-count or parameter-type accuracy to drop by ≥ 20 percentage points, indicating that bytecode-internal constraints are insufficient and that selector resolution is a necessary prerequisite for useful type recovery (i.e., the two subproblems are tightly coupled in practice even if theoretically separable).
motivating_papers: SigRec: Automatic Recovery of Function Signatures in Smart Contracts
Efficient Inference of Static Types for Java Bytecode
Elipmoc: advanced decompilation of Ethereum smart contracts

hypothesis: The Solidity optimizer's effect on ABI recovery mirrors the phenomenon observed in Dalvik-to-native compilation (Lantz & Johansson, "Towards bridging the gap between Dalvik bytecode and native code during static analysis of Android applications"), where compiler transformations reduce analysis accuracy not by destroying information but by redistributing it across a wider code region (inlining dispatch comparisons into caller contexts, merging constant propagation across basic blocks). A finite catalog of pattern-based deoptimization rewrite rules — reversing known Solidity optimizer passes (constant folding, dead-code elimination, expression simplification) — can restore function-entry detection F1 on optimized contracts to within 5% of unoptimized-contract F1.
rationale: Lin & Gao's "When Function Signature Recovery Meets Compiler Optimization" demonstrates that Solidity's --optimize flag systematically breaks SigRec by eliminating dispatch-pattern artifacts. In the Android analysis literature, Lantz & Johansson showed that the gap between Dalvik bytecode and native code is bridgeable through semantics-preserving decompilation passes that reverse known compiler transformations. The Solidity optimizer applies a finite, documented set of transformations (constant propagation, redundant-assignment elimination, expression simplification, dead-code elimination). Each transformation has a well-defined inverse under the condition that the transformation is semantics-preserving (which all Solidity optimizer passes are, by design). A pre-analysis deoptimization pass — analogous to peephole optimization reversal in traditional binary decompilation (Artho & Biere, "Subroutine Inlining and Bytecode Abstraction to Simplify Static and Dynamic Analysis") — should recover dispatch patterns that appear eliminated but are merely transformed into semantically equivalent, structurally obscure forms.
supports_if: Applying a deoptimization pre-pass (reversing known Solidity optimizer transformations via pattern-matching rewrite rules) to a dataset of ≥ 500 optimized contracts brings function-entry detection F1 from the degraded level reported by Lin & Gao to within 5 percentage points of the F1 achieved on the same contracts compiled without --optimize, using the same downstream analysis tool.
refutes_if: No finite set of deoptimization rewrite rules can restore F1 to within 5% of unoptimized levels, OR the Solidity optimizer applies ≥ 3 transformations that are not locally invertible (e.g., branch merging that collapses semantically distinct dispatch paths into a single code path), OR deoptimization requires solving undecidable problems (e.g., alias analysis across storage slots) to a precision that is not achievable at scale.
motivating_papers: When Function Signature Recovery Meets Compiler Optimization
Towards bridging the gap between Dalvik bytecode and native code during static analysis of Android applications
Elipmoc: advanced decompilation of Ethereum smart contracts
Subroutine Inlining and Bytecode Abstraction to Simplify Static and Dynamic Analysis
